title: Hello in Polish: Cześć, Dzień Dobry and When to Use Each
excerpt: Hello in Polish is cześć with friends and dzień dobry with everyone else. Learn how to pronounce each greeting and when to use it.
metaDescription: Hello in Polish is cześć with friends and dzień dobry with everyone else. Pronunciation, formal vs informal, phone greetings, slang and greeting etiquette.
summary: Say dzień dobry (jen DOH-bry) to strangers and anyone you'd call Pan or Pani, and cześć (cheshch) to friends and people on first-name terms.
There is no separate everyday phrase for good morning in Polish: dzień dobry covers the whole day until dobry wieczór takes over in the evening.
Witam is fine when you're the host, but many Poles find it presumptuous at the top of an email, so dzień dobry is the safer opening.
Shake hands with eye contact, save cheek kisses for family and close friends, and never greet anyone across a threshold.
featuredImageAlt: Two friends waving and smiling at each other on a walkway, the kind of casual moment where you'd say hello in Polish with cześć
authorBio: PolishPal Contributor writes about Polish culture, history, and language for learners and the Polish diaspora.
factNotes: Number of cheek kisses: sources disagree (Cultural Atlas/Wikipedia say three on alternating cheeks; Rosetta Stone says one between friends, three for family), so the text says three is the traditional pattern and many younger people do one or a hug. The reply 'Na wieki wieków, amen' to 'Niech będzie pochwalony Jezus Chrystus' is standard Catholic usage from general knowledge; the Szczęść Boże Wikipedia page did not cover it. The 'witam' debate is attributed to Michał Rusinek and Jerzy Bralczyk via bezprawnik.pl (secondary source); I could not open a PWN Poradnia answer directly, so no PWN ruling is claimed. No fixed clock time is given for switching to 'dobry wieczór' because no authoritative source states one. The clipped greeting 'Dobry!' and the 'young teams use cześć from day one' remark are general observations, hedged in the text. Existing post polish-slang glosses siema as short for 'co słychać'; Wiktionary says it clips 'jak się masz', which this post follows (coordinator may want to align the older post). Cheek-kiss count disagreement was seen in search-result summaries of Wikipedia 'Greeting' and a Rosetta Stone blog, which I did not open directly; only the Cultural Atlas page was opened.
